# FM-1 projects

> Drew Robinson's open-source projects for the M-VAVE FM-1, a tiny hardware synthesiser: ESTAMPIE (custom firmware), FM-SWITCH (an iPhone, iPad and Mac app for swapping firmwares) and FM1Kit (the Swift package for installing firmware that the app is built on). None of them is affiliated with M-VAVE.

This file is for language models and other software reading the site at https://fm-1.drewr.dev/. It explains what each project is, how they fit together, and where to find more. Each project's folder also has its own llms-full.txt with more detail.

## The FM-1

The M-VAVE FM-1 is a small, inexpensive hardware synthesiser with a screen, a keyboard and USB-MIDI. It runs on a JieLi AC791N chip. M-VAVE publishes official firmware (V15 is the current official release) and an open-source firmware and updater (fm1_open, Apache-2.0), and a community of custom firmwares has grown around the device: Felucca by Leo Kuroshita (Hügelton Instruments), GHOULBOX by Jason Persinger, X0X, Melodee, Jangada and others. Firmware is distributed as `.fwsc` packages and installed over USB-MIDI by an update protocol, which the community has reverse-engineered (FM-1-RE, https://github.com/AL-255/FM-1-RE).

## How the projects fit together

- ESTAMPIE is a firmware: it runs on the FM-1 itself.
- FM1Kit is a library: it installs any FM-1 firmware (ESTAMPIE, Felucca, M-VAVE's V15 and others) from Apple devices.
- FM-SWITCH is an app built on FM1Kit: it lists the community's firmwares, saves them and installs them, from an iPhone, iPad or Mac.

## Site layout

- `/` : the index, linking to each project.
- `/estampie/` : ESTAMPIE's site, built from the estampie repository: a browser emulator, a web installer, a sound editor, the user guide and firmware downloads.
- `/fm-switch/` : FM-SWITCH's page.
- `/fm1kit/` : FM1Kit's page, an overview of the package's API.
- `/bootloader-check/` : for firmware developers, which firmwares on Felucca's update code trap users with a changed bootloader (m-bootloader, or Open V12/V14's) by only installing other Felucca-based firmwares. Its data is `/bootloader-check/data.json`, with corrections in `/bootloader-check/overrides.json`.
- `/fm1-moment/` : The FM-1 Moment, a dated and sourced history of the FM-1's custom-firmware boom in 2026, as of 1 November 2026. Its dataset of about 200 firmwares' first public releases is `/fm1-moment/releases.csv`.
- `/llms.txt` : a short index of this file.

---

## ESTAMPIE

A mediæval groovebox: custom firmware for the M-VAVE FM-1, named after the estampie, a fast dance of the 13th and 14th centuries. It's for lively mediæval music: tavern and court dances rather than the crypt, with plucked lutes and citoles, buzzing hurdy-gurdies, shawms and bagpipes over drones, frame drums, tabors and nakers, chant, and the church modes.

- Status: 0.3.8, early but ready for use. Done so far: the look (VELLUM: parchment, iron-gall ink, vermilion rubrics, lapis), the screen's type and the illuminated boot screen; KEY TOUCH (velocity and aftertouch from the FM-1's own keys); the screen reader; and the browser emulator, web installer, editor and user guide. The sounds are still mostly GHOULBOX's, with ESTAMPIE's TROTTO scene, DANCE drum kit and mediæval presets.
- Newer FM-1s: from 0.3.8 ESTAMPIE knows the flash chip in FM-1s sold since autumn 2026 (UC25HQ80, JEDEC ID 0xB36014). On those units earlier versions saved nothing past power-off and couldn't be updated over USB. This is not yet tried on a newer FM-1, only on an emulator; it has been tested on an FM-1 with the older chip.
- On USB it shows up as M-VAVE's V15 does, named "FM-1", so a computer keeps the one FM-1 it knows whichever firmware runs.
- Lineage: a fork of GHOULBOX (Jason Persinger's dungeon-synth firmware), itself a fork of Felucca (Leo Kuroshita, Hügelton Instruments), on Felucca 1.6.1. Nearly everything is their work.
- Features: thirteen engines (virtual analog, 6-operator FM, phase distortion, chiptune, real recordings, sung vowels, three oscillators, tonewheel organ, granular, physical models, GHOULBOX's hurdy-gurdy, noise and drums) on four tracks, each with a 64-step sequencer, an arpeggiator, chord keys, scales and mediæval temperaments (Pythagorean, meantone, just). The hurdy-gurdy's drones can keep sounding through the sequencer's rests.
- Licence: GPL-3.0-only, as GHOULBOX and Felucca. Engines from Felucca-Engines are MIT; the Hügelton Sample Pack is CC0 1.0.
- Source: https://github.com/ocean/estampie
- Site: https://fm-1.drewr.dev/estampie/

Inspired by the idea of teenage engineering's EP-1320 medieval; not affiliated with them, and none of their sounds are used.

---

## FM-SWITCH

An app for iPhone, iPad and Mac for swapping M-VAVE FM-1 firmwares over USB.

- Firmwares come from the firmware hub's catalogue (thefirmwarehub.com), fm1-editor.com's list, aroum's FM1 Resource Hub and mutant.cloud, sorted by name, latest update or most installed, with filters for kinds and for firmwares built from source. Each firmware has its own page, with pictures from its README and its links. The app finds each one's package (GitHub releases, publisher manifests, project pages, M-VAVE's downloads), checks for newer releases, and saves firmwares on the device for offline flashing, keeping earlier saved releases too, which a firmware's page switches between. A firmware's details say which FM-1s it saves on.
- M-VAVE's official V15 comes with the app, unmodified (from fm1_open, Apache-2.0), so there's always a known-good firmware to go back to.
- Flashing checks the package first, asks which FM-1 to use when more than one is connected, asks before switching firmware (which can erase the FM-1's projects and samples) and says what switching back will take, keeps the screen awake, can carry on where an interrupted install left off, and is done as soon as the FM-1 starts the new firmware. An install goes through three stages: getting ready, installing and restarting; the FM-1's screen stays dark meanwhile.
- Switching back: when the firmware on the FM-1 won't take the one picked, FM-SWITCH puts MIDIMON on first. It warns before V16 (going back to V15 needs a Mac) and before V15 after V16. Firmwares that only know the older flash chip get a warning, unless the FM-1 says it has the older chip; "How would I know?" explains how to tell (the M-VAVE logo is on the front, under the screen, on FM-1s with the newer chip).
- Save my FM-1: on M-VAVE's open firmware, keeps a copy of the FM-1's projects and samples.
- Look: Standard is friendly and plain, with a warm parchment ground (#EEE8DD), white cards, the system font, purple for firmware (#6D28D9) and a drawn FM-1, in light or dark. Retro, the original 8-bit handheld-console look (green #7BE39A, Silkscreen, Departure Mono and VT323), is hidden until found, then chosen in Settings. The website's FM-SWITCH page has both looks too: https://fm-1.drewr.dev/fm-switch/retro/
- Free: every feature is free, and tips unlock nothing.
- Platforms: iOS and iPadOS 17+, macOS 14+ (native SwiftUI). Connects by USB-C, Lightning with Apple's camera adapter, or a Mac's USB.
- Mac: with the FM-1 in download mode, backs up its whole flash and restores it later, installs M-VAVE's V16 with its own bootloader, and installs m-bootloader 2.1. Each install's log is saved, to send if something goes wrong.
- Status: iPhone and iPad in TestFlight (more on the FM-1 Discord); the Mac app is a signed, notarised download: https://github.com/ocean/FM-SWITCH/releases/latest/download/FM-SWITCH.dmg
- Source: https://github.com/ocean/FM-SWITCH (MPL-2.0)
- Page: https://fm-1.drewr.dev/fm-switch/

---

## FM1Kit

A Swift package for installing firmware on the M-VAVE FM-1 over USB-MIDI, from iOS and macOS, with a second library, FM1Rescue, for rescuing it in the chip's USB download mode from a Mac.

- It reads `.fwsc` firmware packages, finds the device, answers its read requests while it stages and writes the new firmware, and checks the device reports the new firmware afterwards. It can finish an update that was cut off, or one started from USB recovery mode, can restore V15's 128 factory voices, and can back up M-VAVE's open firmware (its 16 project slots, the project being edited and the sample bank) as files M-VAVE's workbench can restore. With several FM-1s connected, `devices()` lists them to choose from.
- `LeavingGuide`: before a firmware is installed, it reads the package to work out how that firmware installs others, and combines that with the FM-1's bootloader to give the route back to V15, V16, open firmware, other custom firmwares and m-bootloader, with warnings to show first and step-by-step instructions. It's `Codable`, so apps can save it with the FM-1.
- M-VAVE's V16 is recognised as an official release, but only V15 may be included in an app; V16 is downloaded from M-VAVE.
- It knows both FM-1 flash chips: the first units' P25Q80 (0x856014) and the UC25HQ80 (0xB36014) in those sold since autumn 2026, from firmwares that report it, and which chips a package supports. Firmwares built on felucca-bsp since November 2026 shorten their identity in the handshake, so it asks them for the whole of it. Not yet tried on an FM-1 with the newer chip.
- An install finishes when the new firmware answers, even if the loader never asks to finish. If an install is interrupted while writing, the FM-1's screen stays dark: keep it switched on and resume.
- From V15 it installs m-bootloader (https://github.com/jvitkauskas/m-bootloader, MIT), keeping the firmware: hold PLAY while switching on for its recovery menu, or REC for download mode. Installing V15 later puts M-VAVE's bootloader back.
- For apps aimed at everyone: `InstallProgress` (one progress bar in three stages that never goes backwards: getting ready, installing, restarting), `FM1Advice` (any error as a headline, an explanation, whether the FM-1 is still fine, and one action) and `FM1Updater.summary()` (the firmware's name and version, whether it's waiting mid-update, the USB serial number and, where reported, the flash chip).
- FM1Rescue (macOS only, empty on iOS, needs root, so apps reach it through a privileged helper) works whatever firmware is installed. It backs up the 1 MB flash, reading it twice and checking both against the chip's CRC-32, saved as M-Flasher saves it. `FlashPlan` restores a backup, installs m-bootloader or M-VAVE's bootloader, or installs a firmware (optionally erasing every firmware's saved data), writing only the 4 KB sectors that change, from the top of the flash down so start-up code is replaced last, and checking each one. `USBDownloadModeConnection.open(waitingUpTo:)` catches an FM-1 that only passes through download mode, as one stuck restarting does. Another FM-1's backup never replaces this one's factory data.
- Main types: `FwscPackage`, `LeavingGuide`, `OfficialFirmware`, `FM1Identity`, `FM1FlashChip`, `FM1Updater` (an actor), `InstallCheck`, `InstallOptions`, `UpdateEvent`, `FM1Capability`, `FM1BuildID`, `OpenFirmwareBackup`, `OpenFirmwareProject`, `BootloaderInstaller`, `BootloaderImage`, `InstallProgress`, `FM1Advice`, `FM1DeviceSummary`, `CoreMIDITransport`, `SimulatedFM1`; in FM1Rescue, `USBDownloadModeConnection`, `FlashSession`, `FlashBackup`, `FlashPlan`, `SimulatedDownloadMode`.
- Also ships `fm1probe`, a Mac command-line tool for listing ports and FM-1s, identifying the device, inspecting packages, installing, backing up open firmware, installing m-bootloader, and backing up, restoring and writing the flash in download mode.
- Requirements: iOS 17 or macOS 14, Swift 6.1 or later.
- Install: `.package(url: "https://github.com/ocean/FM1Kit.git", .upToNextMinor(from: "0.6.0"))`
- Status: 0.6.0, tested on one FM-1 so far, from both a Mac and an iPhone. Download mode has been tested from a Mac: backups, restoring V15 over Felucca, installing Felucca, and swapping bootloaders, ending byte for byte as it started.
- Licence: MIT. Contains no M-VAVE firmware and no code from GPL-licensed installers.
- Source: https://github.com/ocean/FM1Kit
- Page: https://fm-1.drewr.dev/fm1kit/

---

## Bootloader check

A page for FM-1 firmware developers, at https://fm-1.drewr.dev/bootloader-check/.

- The safety check: Felucca's update code, in `ota_stage()` (`firmware/src/ota.c`), compares the first 0x4000 bytes of a package that brings M-VAVE's update loader with the FM-1's boot area, and returns -5 ("UPDATE / CHECK HEAD / FAILED") at the first difference; any other writer that isn't Felucca's own loader is refused too, with -3 when the package has no flash.bin (as m-bootloader's installer has none; tested on hardware, with nothing shown on Felucca 1.6.1's screen) or -7 when it has one (from code reading). Felucca's own loader has no boot-area check. So on an FM-1 with a changed bootloader, the firmware traps its users. With m-bootloader, which never matches, it only installs other Felucca-based firmwares over USB: V15, M-VAVE's open firmware V12/V14 and non-Felucca firmwares are refused, and the ways to switch are a Felucca-based firmware with the updated check, which can then install V15, or download mode (tested on hardware). After Open V12/V14, which writes its own boot area that a Felucca-based firmware then keeps, V15 is refused; copies before Felucca 1.6.1 can install Open again and go to V15 from there, but 1.6.1-based copies also refuse Open (-15, shown as "FAILED -15"), so the only way out over USB is through a firmware with the updated check (tested on hardware with Open V12; V14's boot area is identical). m-bootloader itself works correctly and isn't at fault. It's a sensible safeguard that assumes M-VAVE's original bootloader is the only one, not a bug. Nothing is written before the check.
- The updated check: felucca-bsp commit afd83ede (https://github.com/hugelton/felucca-bsp/commit/afd83ede, by Charles Vestal) adds `ota_boot_valid()`, which accepts any package whose bootloader is a valid FM-1 one, and any well-formed writer. The commit also relaxes -3 to need only the writer (`if (!ota_off)`), so a package with no flash.bin, such as m-bootloader's installer, gets through. Copies based on Felucca 1.6.1 have one more check, which the commit doesn't touch: a flash.bin that isn't 0x93000 bytes returns -15, which stops Open V12/V14 (0x6F000 and 0x73000). Check it only when there's a flash.bin (`if (fl_off && fl_len != OTA_FL_LEN)`). Port it into your `ota.c`, or update fm1-base to 6c0b47e or felucca-bsp to afd83ede or later. Felucca's main branch doesn't include it yet.
- The list: every public FM-1 firmware on Felucca's update code, with its main branch's status and its latest release package's status, rechecked by a scheduled job. Corrections go in by pull request to `bootloader-check/overrides.json` in https://github.com/ocean/fm1-site.

---

## Safety and affiliation

Installing custom firmware on an FM-1 is at the owner's own risk. If an FM-1 doesn't start after an update, some firmwares offer USB recovery mode (hold OCT− while switching it on), and FM1Kit's resume can install a firmware whenever the device is in its update loader. Beyond that, the chip's USB download mode works whatever the firmware, from a computer: FM1Kit's FM1Rescue on a Mac, or M-Flasher (https://github.com/jvitkauskas/m-flasher). M-VAVE's own updater returns an FM-1 to stock firmware. M-VAVE and FM-1 are trademarks of their respective owners; none of these projects is affiliated with or endorsed by M-VAVE.
